messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Please, I want . . .
parts:
So, I was running Stan from R and typing the usual thing:

stan(…, data=list(y=y, N=N, …))

or

stan(…, data=c(“y”,”N”,…))

And I realized (again) that R (or, I assume, Py and J and …) should be able to do this automatically by just reading off the variable names in the data block of the Stan program and looking for the objects in the workspace. (And, if some of the objs are not there, they could be added in the call.) Thus, e.g.,

stan(…) with no “data” argument would just pull everything out of the workspace and return an error if anything’s missing or is the wrong type

stan(…, data=list(y=y, N=50)) would use the specified data for y and N and pull all the other data out of the workspace, etc.

This would make a huge difference and should be really easy, no?

A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Please, I want . . .
parts:
The first part of what Andrew wants (almost) works now, using

data = globalenv()

in the call. I suppose the RStan devs could make that the default,
then Andrew would get to do exactly what he wants.

I believe it will fail if there are certain things in the global
environment that RStan can't deal with in terms of reading them as data.

I'm not an R expert, but I'm thinking if RStan would define the var_context
to pull from the global environment as variables are needed, then this
caveat could be removed.

The second thing Andrew wants also (almost) works, but not as is.
You need to define a new environment, with the global as default
parent, then assign in that new environment and pass it in.

> sigma <- 4
> e <- new.env()
> e$mu <- 2

Then if you use data=e, you will get mu = 2 and sigma = 4.

And again, I see now reason why rS couldn't give An exactly what
he wants.

Now whether it should is another matter. Using globals this way is
dangerous because junk lying around in the environment will be
inadvertently brought in and used to define data accidentally. Also,
any scripts using this technique will likely be completely non-reproducible
by the next person because they'll forget to include the data definitions.

I'd personally rather encourage hygienic and reproducible programming
habits.

- Bob

On Friday, April 3, 2015 at 11:26:09 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Now whether it should is another matter.  Using globals this way is
dangerous because junk lying around in the environment will be
inadvertently brought in and used to define data accidentally.  Also,
any scripts using this technique will likely be completely non-reproducible

Also, it presumes that stan() is being called by the user directly as opposed to some other function that wants to use the symbols from its environment rather than the global environment. I suppose Andrew would say that those scripts should pass the data explicitly (and they probably should). But those scripts would say Andrew should pass .GlobalEnv explicitly, which he should. messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Please, I want . . .
parts:
I agree with Andrew that this would be nice, but I also agree with Ben about not messing too much with R's scoping rules. So I guess I don't have too much to add.

As a somewhat related aside, instead of using

data = list(y = y, N = N, ...) or data = c("y", "N", ...)

I wrote a function nlist, which is equivalent to list() except that if you don't include names it automatically uses the name of the objects with missing names. For example,

stan(..., data = nlist(y, N))

and

stan(..., data = nlist(y, N=50))

are both fine. It's not a huge improvement over list() or c() but it lets you be a bit lazier. I've also found that this nlist function is pretty useful for many non-Stan R tasks.

nlist <- function(...) {
m <- match.call()
out <- list(...)
no_names <- is.null(names(out))
has_name <- if (no_names) FALSE else nzchar(names(out))
if (all(has_name)) return(out)
nms <- as.character(m)[-1]
if (no_names) {
names(out) <- nms
} else {
names(out)[!has_name] <- nms[!has_name]
}
out
}

(I haven't tested it thoroughly but I think it should work in all cases.)

And I realized (again) that R (or, I assume, Py and J and …) should be able to do this automatically by just reading off the variable names in the data block of the Stan program and looking for the objects in the workspace.

Good idea.  But for now, the C++ class model generated from our parser, stanc, does not provide a function to get the names and/or dimensions, so even though they are written in data block, they are still unknown in general.  (And if we are gonna add such function, I think it should be static). 

And passing .GlobalEnv by default is not a good idea since there is a preprocess of the data, which needs to check all the NA/NaN in the data and set data to integer types if there is no loss of precision.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: lazy var_context for R
parts:
I changed topic because Michael should read this and
Andrew shouldn't bother.

> On Apr 4, 2015, at 12:08 PM, Jiqiang Guo <guo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> On Fri, Apr 3, 2015 at 10:27 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> And I realized (again) that R (or, I assume, Py and J and …) should be able to do this automatically by just reading off the variable names in the data block of the Stan program and looking for the objects in the workspace.
>
> Good idea. But for now, the C++ class model generated from our parser, stanc, does not provide a function to get the names and/or dimensions, so even though they are written in data block, they are still unknown in general. (And if we are gonna add such function, I think it should be static).

Right --- there's no function to get it. I could add something
static to provide names and dimensions, but sizes are dynamic.
But I don't think that's needed here.

> And passing .GlobalEnv by default is not a good idea since there is a preprocess of the data, which needs to check all the NA/NaN in the data and set data to integer types if there is no loss of precision.

Thanks for explaining what can go wrong here.

Is there no way to make the var_context implementation do all this work lazily
rather than building it all up in memory ahead of time?

I think there are two advantages:

1. no duplication of data, and

2. no problems with extraneous variables passed in possibly being undefined
or having NaN or NA values.

It should be possible because the constructor for the generated program
class will attempt to pull each item out of the var_context. At the
point the constructor tries to pull the data values from the var_context,
it tells the var_context what the sizes are.

It would require a custom implementation of var_context on the R side that
knows how to read from an R environment. Then if you passed in variable
definitions (e.g., list(a=3, b=c(1,23)), the values would go in the environment.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Please, I want . . .
parts:
On Friday, April 3, 2015 at 11:15:48 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
First, data=globalenv() is confusing for me.  I don’t necessarily want stan() to use the _global_ environment.  I want it to use whatever environment I’m calling it from. If I’m calling Stan from a function, or from a loop, or whatever, I’d like it to use whatever R would be using, and I’d like that to be the default.  This would perhaps deal with Ben’s objection.

On one hand, it would be good to make Stan behave more like lm() and glm() where the variables are searched for starting in the environment of the formula. We don't have explicit formulas, but we do know that the implicit formula involves all of the objects in the data block of the Stan program.

On the other hand ...

Second, I want to encourage hygienic and reproducible programming habits too.  And the current way it’s done is _not_ “hygenic and reproducible.”  The current approach is I have to read the data block in the Stan program, then retype them all as data in the stan() call, thus data(list(y=y,N=N,…)).  That’s super unhygenic because it copies code.  It means that when I change my Stan program I need to change the call, it’s horrible.

There are many exceptions, but I would guess the majority of the time this is self-inflicted and a consequence of writing the data block like

data {
  int<lower =1> N;
  vector<lower=0> age;
  vector<lower=0> income;
  ...
  int<lower=0,upper=1> vote[N];
}

instead of

data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> K;
  matrix[N,K] X;
  int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];
}

I really discourage the former in my class because the resulting .stan program is not generic enough. If we implement Andrew's suggestion, then it is going to increase (perhaps drastically) the proportion of non-generic, BUGS-like .stan programs. But non-generic, BUGS-like .stan programs are legal in Stan, and I don't like not implementing useful features for fear they will get misused, even if the fear is well-founded.

So, does anyone object to calling something like this and overwriting with anything passed through the data argument to stan(), sampling(), etc.? There may be a better way to get the names of the objects in the data block once Michael's refactoring lands.

parse_data <- function(program, e = parent.frame()) {
  lines <- readLines(program)
  # find the line that has "data {"
  data_mark <- grep("^[[:blank:]]*data[[:blank:]]*\\{[[:blank:]]*$", lines)
  # find the first line that only has "}"
  end_data_mark <- data_mark +
    grep("^[[:blank:]]*\\}[[:blank:]]*$", lines[-c(1:data_mark)])[1]
  # pull out object names from the data block
  objects <- gsub("^.* ([0-9A-Za-z_]+).*;.*$", "\\1",
                  lines[(data_mark+1L):(end_data_mark-1L)])
  # get them from the calling environment
  mget(objects, envir = e, inherits = TRUE,
       ifnotfound = rep(NA_real_, length(objects)))
}

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Please, I want . . .
parts:
> On Apr 4, 2015, at 2:15 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> OK, now let me give the user’s perspective.

I understand that everything you're saying is from your
perspective as a user. And partly my objection is not to
Andrew's feature request, but to R's scoping rules and how
they're used interactively.

R's scoping lets a function's scope grab variables out of
containing environments, as in:

> f <- function(x) { x + zzz; }

> f(3)
Error in f(3) : object 'zzz' not found

> zzz <- 12

> f(3)

[1] 15

Because R is interpreted, people (myself included, I'm ashamed
to admit) often use it interactively to define variables on the fly,
rather than running everything out of a script in a clean environment.
RStudio explicitly supports this by making it easy to evaluate fragments
of a program in the global environment. Other users cut-and-paste, or
use the history with slight edits.

Putting R's scoping and interactive cut-and-paste-and-update together
leads to the non-reproducibility issues I'm worried about.

The only way to combat this of which I'm aware is to run everything
out of a script file in a clean environment. If a program works that
way, it's good to go (assuming any data it reads is distributed along
with the script).

Now onto Andrew's preferred programming practice with RStan.

Do you (Andrew) always work by first defining every variable in
the Stan data block in the environment from which you call stan()?
Do you think that's what we should be encouraging everyone to do?
It's not what I tend to do, but I may very well be an outlier.

If so, then I agree that following the R2WinBUGS idiom of
forcing users to type data = list(a=a, b=b,...) is redundant.
I wouldn't call it "horrible", though, because it's the standard
way of calling functions in R and following the idioms of a language
makes programs more readable. Specifying all the data variables
explicitly makes it clear what's getting passed in. Neither of these are
intrinsically bad.

The introduction of data = c("a", "b", ...) was meant to cut
down on typing in the situation where variables are all defined
in the calling environment.

Jonah's nlist() function goes even further and has the useful
property that you can provide partial overrides, defining some
variables in the call and grabbing the rest from the environment.

> First, data=globalenv() is confusing for me. I don’t necessarily want stan() to use the _global_ environment. I want it to use whatever environment I’m calling it from. If I’m calling Stan from a function, or from a loop, or whatever, I’d like it to use whatever R would be using, and I’d like that to be the default. This would perhaps deal with Ben’s objection.

Calling with data = environment() would use the current environment.
This cuts down typing even further and avoids having to enumerate the
names of the variables in the Stan program, which I know Andrew's objected
to before on many occasions.

Then, if environment() is the default value for data, Andrew gets exactly
what he wants, right?

The only problem is that it won't work now if the environment isn't
clean. That's a positive in my mind, but then I'm a neat freak who
wants everyone to be a tidy programmer and not leave their dirty
variables (laundry) lying around in the environment (on the floor).
I think requiring a clean environment may be a dealbreaker for Andrew,
which is why I brought up a way to read data more lazily and make sure
only the variables in the Stan program get read out of the
environment (right now, everything from the environment is converted
to input and if any of them have NaN or NA you get an error, and if
any have string data, you get warnings).

None of these steps cuts down on my concern about the scope of R and
the habit of interactively updating environments. In fact, I think
it encourages what I take to be dangerous programming practices.

But hey, that's just me and I realize I'm a worry wart and a neat freak.

> Second, I want to encourage hygienic and reproducible programming habits too. And the current way it’s done is _not_ “hygenic and reproducible.” The current approach is I have to read the data block in the Stan program, then retype them all as data in the stan() call, thus data(list(y=y,N=N,…)). That’s super unhygenic because it copies code. It means that when I change my Stan program I need to change the call, it’s horrible.

Could you give an example of the before and after Stan program and
what the environment looks like that works for both? I don't understand
what you'd like to be able to do and how reading out of the current
environment would support it.

Now for what I want as a user. I'd like to read a dump file into a list
then call stan() with that list as data. I don't know how to do that
in R, though. This would make it easy to use R data + program across
Stan interfaces and would ensure that everything's neatly reproducible.
At least assuming you check the latest script and data into version control
and tag which version is used to generate the data for a paper or whatever.

- Bob

> Now for what I want as a user. I'd like to read a dump file into a list
> then call stan() with that list as data. I don't know how to do that
> in R, though. This would make it easy to use R data + program across
> Stan interfaces and would ensure that everything's neatly reproducible.
> At least assuming you check the latest script and data into version control

Bob, you mean like this?

setwd(‘/path/to/current/directory')
data <- read_rdump(‘data/model.stan.data')
fit <- stan(file=‘model.stan', data=data, …)

You can do the same thing in PyStan, too,

data = pystan.read_rdump(‘data/model.stan.data')
fit = pystan.stan(file=‘model.stan', data=data, …)

This is how I work with the interfaces because it allows
me to use the same common data file.

I have to admit that I am incredibly opposed to having the entire
environment be the default, if only because then the mailing list
will be full of people sending scripts of failing models that we
can’t run because the environment is different. Retyping may
lead to the occasional typo, but at least that typo will be the
same for everyone so we can readily diagnose it!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Please, I want . . .
parts:
> On Apr 5, 2015, at 1:20 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
>> Now for what I want as a user. I'd like to read a dump file into a list
>> then call stan() with that list as data. I don't know how to do that
>> in R, though. This would make it easy to use R data + program across
>> Stan interfaces and would ensure that everything's neatly reproducible.
>> At least assuming you check the latest script and data into version control
>> and tag which version is used to generate the data for a paper or whatever.
>
> Bob, you mean like this?
>
> setwd(‘/path/to/current/directory')
> data <- read_rdump(‘data/model.stan.data')
> fit <- stan(file=‘model.stan', data=data, …)

Awesome. That's exactly what I wanted to do. I was
looking for something generic to read into a list,
not realizing RStan had something that did it.

> You can do the same thing in PyStan, too,
>
> data = pystan.read_rdump(‘data/model.stan.data')
> fit = pystan.stan(file=‘model.stan', data=data, …)
>
> This is how I work with the interfaces because it allows
> me to use the same common data file.

Exactly why I want it. That, and because it lets me
save everything in an easy-to-reuse way.

> I have to admit that I am incredibly opposed to having the entire
> environment be the default, if only because then the mailing list
> will be full of people sending scripts of failing models that we
> can’t run because the environment is different. Retyping may
> lead to the occasional typo, but at least that typo will be the
> same for everyone so we can readily diagnose it!

That's Andrew's wish, not mine. I've never seen anyone use
the explicit environment option that's already there, but it might
get more popular if it's implemented to be lazy.

My wish was for a read_rdump function and it's been granted!

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Please, I want . . .
parts:
Hi, see comments below.
A

> On Apr 4, 2015, at 2:11 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> Jonah's nlist() function goes even further and has the useful
> property that you can provide partial overrides, defining some
> variables in the call and grabbing the rest from the environment.

I agree that nlist() is fine, I guess I’d just like something that did this automatically so I didn’t have to hunt thru my stan program and be careful to declare all the damn variables.

But I agree with Ben that this shouldn’t be a _requirement_, for example we might want the call to look like data=list(y=vote, N=length(vote), x=income, etc).

>> First, data=globalenv() is confusing for me. I don’t necessarily want stan() to use the _global_ environment. I want it to use whatever environment I’m calling it from. If I’m calling Stan from a function, or from a loop, or whatever, I’d like it to use whatever R would be using, and I’d like that to be the default. This would perhaps deal with Ben’s objection.
>
> Calling with data = environment() would use the current environment.
OK, that sounds good. I’m pretty R-ignorant and didn’t know about environment(). I’ll try it out.

> This cuts down typing even further and avoids having to enumerate the
> names of the variables in the Stan program, which I know Andrew's objected
> to before on many occasions.
>
> Then, if environment() is the default value for data, Andrew gets exactly
> what he wants, right?
>
> The only problem is that it won't work now if the environment isn't
> clean. That's a positive in my mind, but then I'm a neat freak who
> wants everyone to be a tidy programmer and not leave their dirty
> variables (laundry) lying around in the environment (on the floor).
> I think requiring a clean environment may be a dealbreaker for Andrew,
If anything is needed for the Stan code but it’s not in the R environment (or not the right size as specified in the Stan program), then the stan call will return an error, so that’s ok.

>
>> Second, I want to encourage hygienic and reproducible programming habits too. And the current way it’s done is _not_ “hygenic and reproducible.” The current approach is I have to read the data block in the Stan program, then retype them all as data in the stan() call, thus data(list(y=y,N=N,…)). That’s super unhygenic because it copies code. It means that when I change my Stan program I need to change the call, it’s horrible.
>
> Could you give an example of the before and after Stan program and
> what the environment looks like that works for both? I don't understand
> what you'd like to be able to do and how reading out of the current
> environment would support it.
I’m happy with data=environment() and I’m happy with data=list(y=vote, N=length(vote), x=income, etc)

messages.author: 83aa4ea66d984b54
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Please, I want . . .
parts:
I've put some of that into StataStan (it was Ben's suggestion really) but only as an option, so you can type matrices(all) and get, errr... all the matrices. But it won't do it unless you type (all). We could add that for variables in the current data file too.

My reason for being a little wary was confidentiality of data. Someone might get upset at having accidentally published their Stan data, containing some sensitive information that they hadn't meant to release.
